lead: A bolted bracket rarely pulls at the centre of its bolt group. The load arrives off-centre, so each bolt feels a direct share plus a turning share. Move the load to the group centroid, split it into a force and a moment, calculate each bolt's share, then add the two as vectors. The worst bolt sizes the joint. Machine frames, motor mounts, pipe flanges and payment-terminal housings use this idea.
prereq: You need Unit 1's direct shear, tension, eccentric loading and principal stresses.

sections.h3: Thread terms and the stress area

blocks.text: A screw thread has three diameters. The major diameter d is the largest. The minor diameter d₁ is the smallest, at the thread root. The pitch diameter lies between them, where thread thickness equals gap. Pitch p is the axial distance between adjacent threads. Lead l is the axial advance in one turn. For a single-start thread l = p; for a double-start thread l = 2p.
The thread root reduces the tension area. Design uses the tensile stress area A<sub>s</sub> for ISO metric threads:

blocks.where: A<sub>s</sub> is tensile stress area in mm²; d is nominal major diameter in mm; p is pitch in mm.

blocks.text: Use standard table values of A<sub>s</sub>. The minor-area circle πd₁²/4 is smaller and is not the standard design area for a bolt in tension.
A bolt is tightened before external load arrives. This clamp force is preload F<sub>i</sub>. Tightening torque includes thread friction and friction under the nut or bolt head.

blocks.where: T is tightening torque in N·mm; K is torque coefficient, about 0.2 for dry steel; d is nominal diameter in mm; F<sub>i</sub> is preload in N.

blocks.text: In a shear joint, preload clamps the plates. External shear is carried by friction until slip. After slip, bolts carry shear by bearing and dowel action. In a tension joint, external load adds to bolt tension; check using A<sub>s</sub>. A joint with shear and tension is checked for each effect and their interaction.
An eccentric shear load is handled in five steps, working in the plane of the joint.

items: Find the centroid of the bolt group, not the centroid of the bracket.
Replace load F by the same force at the centroid plus moment M = F e, where e is the perpendicular distance from the centroid to the load line.
Give every bolt primary shear F<sub>p</sub> = F/n, parallel to F. Here n is the number of bolts.

Give bolt i secondary shear F<sub>si</sub> = M r<sub>i</sub> / Σr<sub>i</sub>², perpendicular to the radius from the centroid. Here r<sub>i</sub> is the bolt distance from the centroid in mm, and Σr<sub>i</sub>² is the sum of r² over all bolts in mm².
Add primary and secondary shears as vectors at each bolt. The largest resultant magnitude is the design shear.

blocks.where: F<sub>s</sub> is secondary shear on one bolt in N; M is moment about the centroid in N·mm; r is that bolt's distance from the centroid in mm; Σr² is the sum of squares of all bolt distances in mm².

blocks.text: The direction of Fs follows the moment. For a clockwise moment, secondary shear on a bolt at (x, y) has direction (y, −x). Resolve Fp and Fs into x and y components, add, then take the square root of the sum of squares. The worst bolt is often not the farthest bolt, because the angle between vectors matters. The same centroid-and-moment method applies to welded joints under axial and eccentric loads.

When the moment bends the joint about an axis in its plane, bolts on one side stretch more than those on the other. For a symmetric bolt group the neutral axis passes through the centroid. The total external tensile force on bolt i has a direct part and a moment part:

blocks.where: F<sub>b,i</sub> is total external tensile force in bolt i in N; F is eccentric tensile load in N; n is number of bolts; M = F e is bending moment in N·mm; y<sub>i</sub> is signed distance from the neutral axis in mm; Σy<sub>i</sub>² is the sum over all bolts in mm².

blocks.text: Add this total external tensile force to preload when checking the tension-side bolt. Use A<sub>s</sub>, not the nominal shank area. If the bolt group is not symmetric, the neutral axis shifts; then y must be measured from the shifted axis, not from the centroid.

figure.caption: The load is moved to the centroid and split into a direct shear and a moment; the moment adds a secondary shear, and the vector sum at the worst bolt gives the design load.

spec.title: Eccentric bolted bracket
spec.aria: An eccentric load is moved to the bolt centroid, split into direct and moment shares, and combined into the maximum bolt load.

examples.question: A bracket is held by four bolts at the corners of a 100 mm × 200 mm rectangle. A vertical load F = 12 kN acts at a horizontal distance e = 250 mm from the bolt-group centroid. Take the bolt coordinates as (±50, ±100) mm. Find the maximum shear force in a bolt. The load lies in the plane of the bracket.
steps: Number of bolts n = 4. Centroid at (0, 0). Load F = 12 000 N. Eccentricity e = 250 mm.
Primary shear on every bolt: F_p = F/n = 12 000/4 = 3 000 N = 3.0 kN, downward.
Moment about the centroid: M = F e = 12 000 × 250 = 3 000 000 N·mm = 3.0 kN·m, clockwise.
Sum of squares of bolt distances: Σr² = 4(50² + 100²) = 4(2 500 + 10 000) = 50 000 mm².

All four corner bolts have r = √(50² + 100²) = 111.8 mm and equal secondary shear magnitude. After vector addition, the largest resultant occurs at the two bolts at x = +50 for the assumed clockwise moment.
Secondary shear at (50, 100): F_s = M r/Σr² = 3 000 000 × 111.8/50 000 = 6 708 N = 6.71 kN. Its direction is perpendicular to the radius, clockwise: components (6.0, −3.0) kN.
Add primary shear (0, −3.0) kN: resultant at (50, 100) is (6.0, −6.0) kN. Magnitude = √(6.0² + 6.0²) = 8.49 kN. The bolt at (50, −100) gives the same magnitude.
The maximum bolt shear is therefore 8.49 kN.
examples.answer: The maximum shear force in a bolt is 8.49 kN, at the two bolts at x = +50 mm on the loaded side of the group.
examples.check:
import math
F=12000.0; e=250.0; n=4
M=F*e
s=4*(50**2+100**2)
r=math.hypot(50,100)
Fs=M*r/s
Fp=F/n
Rx=Fs*(100/r)
Ry=-Fs*(50/r)-Fp
R=math.hypot(Rx,Ry)
print(f'{M/1e6:.1f}')
print(f'{r:.1f}')
print(f'{Fs/1000:.2f}')
print(f'{Fp/1000:.1f}')
print(f'{R/1000:.2f}')

traps: Adding primary and secondary shears as scalars. They are vectors at an angle, so resolve into components at the worst bolt.
Measuring r from the load point instead of the bolt-group centroid. The moment is about the centroid.
Using the nominal bolt diameter or shank area for tensile stress. Use the tensile stress area A<sub>s</sub>.
Assuming the farthest bolt is always worst. The vector angle can make a nearer bolt carry more.
In eccentric tension, using y from the centroid when the bolt group is not symmetric. The neutral axis shifts.

quiz.q: Define pitch and lead of a screw thread.
quiz.a: Pitch is the axial distance between adjacent threads. Lead is the axial advance in one complete turn. For a single-start thread lead equals pitch; for a double-start thread lead equals twice the pitch.

quiz.q: Why is the tensile stress area A<sub>s</sub> used instead of πd²/4 for a bolt in tension?
quiz.a: The thread roots reduce the load-carrying area, and the thread form is not a plain cylinder. A<sub>s</sub> is an effective area based on thread geometry and standard tables, so it gives a realistic tensile stress.

quiz.q: A bolt group has Σr² = 40 000 mm² and the farthest bolt is at r = 100 mm. The moment about the centroid is M = 2 kN·m. Find the secondary shear on that bolt.
Four bolts lie at (±40, ±60) mm. A vertical load F = 8 kN acts at e = 150 mm horizontally from the centroid. Find the maximum bolt shear.
quiz.a: F<sub>p</sub> = 8/4 = 2 kN. M = 8 000 × 150 = 1.2 × 10⁶ N·mm. Σr² = 4(40² + 60²) = 20 800 mm². r<sub>max</sub> = 72.11 mm. F<sub>s</sub> = 1.2 × 10⁶ × 72.11/20 800 = 4.16 kN. At (40, 60), secondary components are (3.46, −2.31) kN; adding (0, −2) kN gives (3.46, −4.31) kN. Resultant = 5.53 kN.

quiz.q: Why can the worst bolt in an eccentric shear joint be nearer than the farthest bolt?
quiz.a: The total bolt force is the vector sum of primary and secondary shears. Primary shear is the same on all bolts. Secondary shear grows with r, but its direction changes with position. At a nearer bolt the two vectors may be more closely aligned, giving a larger resultant than at the farthest bolt.

quiz.q: What does the coefficient K ≈ 0.2 in T = K d F<sub>i</sub> include?
quiz.a: It lumps thread friction, friction under the nut or bolt head, and thread geometry. It is not a pure friction coefficient.

quiz.q: A preloaded bolted joint in shear slips. What changes in the load path?
quiz.a: Before slip, shear is carried mainly by friction between clamped plates. After slip, plates move and bolts carry shear by bearing and dowel action. The bolts then see shear and bending, and the joint may lose clamp load.

quiz.q: Write the torque-tension relation for tightening a bolt.
quiz.a: T = K d F<sub>i</sub>, where T is tightening torque, K is torque coefficient, d is nominal diameter and F<sub>i</sub> is preload.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry checks bolted joints with detailed preload and slip calculations, often using VDI 2230-style methods. Finite element models are used for stiff brackets where the centroid method is too simple. Fatigue of bolts, relaxation of preload and vibration loosening are major research topics.
